title: Packet Sniffing and Spoofing Lab
description: Eight automatically graded missions on packet sniffing and spoofing (SEED Labs): Scapy, BPF filters, ICMP spoofing, traceroute, sniff-then-spoof, libpcap, Telnet eavesdropping and C raw sockets. Every sandbox has its own flags.
outcomes: Explain how packet sniffing and packet spoofing work.
Capture and filter traffic with Scapy, tcpdump, Wireshark, and libpcap.
Construct and analyze ICMP and IP packets.
Understand TTL-based traceroute and ICMP responses.
Inspect plaintext Telnet traffic in an isolated lab.
Use C raw sockets and libpcap to implement basic network tools.

levels.title: Introduction and safety rules
levels.content:
# Network Security Practical Challenge

You are a junior network security analyst in an isolated training network. You capture traffic, forge packets and write small network tools. Every mission ends with a **flag** that the lab itself releases, and **flags are different in every sandbox**.

## Rules
- Do all sniffing and spoofing only inside this sandbox. Never send forged packets to public systems.
- You work **only on the `attacker` machine** (SEED Ubuntu 20.04). `client`, `server` and `router` are *user machines*: you reach them with packets, never with a shell.
- Ask the client to generate the traffic of a mission with `lab-trigger <id>` (try `lab-trigger list`).
- `lab-iface` prints the name of the lab network interface. Sniffing and spoofing need root (`sudo`).
- In the traffic a flag looks like `FLAG(M1)=<value>`. **Submit only `<value>`.** Traffic that does not belong to the mission carries look-alike values that are wrong.

## Network map (10.1.26.0/24)
| Machine | Address | Role |
|---|---|---|
| attacker | 10.1.26.10 | your SEED workstation |
| client | 10.1.26.11 | user machine, generates traffic |
| server | 10.1.26.12 | user machine, answers some packets |
| router | 10.1.26.1 | gateway to the Internet and to a simulated remote network (172.31.0.0/16) |

## Grading
The eight missions are worth **20 points** in total (the platform shows 200 internal points: divide by 10). Hints cost 0.5, 1 and 2 points at most; asking for a solution costs the whole mission. A mission never goes below 0. The concept questions of the lab handout go into your written report and do not change the practical grade.

levels.title: Get access to the SEED workstation
levels.cloud_content:
Your first task is to access the sandbox where you will complete all following tasks. After you have connected, submit the answer **`start`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview on the right, right-click on **`attacker`** and choose **Open GUI** (or connect over SSH).
2. Log in with username **`seed`** and password **`dees`**.

You work only on `attacker`. Run `lab-trigger list` in a terminal to see the traffic scenarios; starter code and a short reference are in `~/lab`.
levels.local_content: Cloud sandbox access is required for this scenario.

levels.title: Mission 1 – Sniff ICMP packets with Scapy
levels.content:
## Objective
Capture ICMP echo requests with Scapy and find the flag that is addressed **to your machine**.

1. Find the lab interface: `lab-iface`. The starter `~/lab/sniffer.py` already sniffs ICMP.
2. Run your sniffer as root: `sudo python3 sniffer.py`.
3. In another terminal run `lab-trigger m1`. The client sends echo requests to several destinations.
4. Read the `Raw` payload of the right packets: `FLAG(M1)=<value>`.

**Submit:** the value (without `FLAG(M1)=`).
levels.solution: Run `sudo python3 sniffer.py` (sniff(iface=lab-iface, filter='icmp and dst host 10.1.26.10', prn=...)), then `lab-trigger m1`. Print `pkt[Raw].load`; the real flag is in the packets sent to 10.1.26.10. Submit the part after `FLAG(M1)=`.

hints.title: Which packets?
hints.content: The client also pings another machine of the lab. Look at the destination address of every packet.

hints.title: How to filter
hints.content: A BPF filter can keep only the packets addressed to you, e.g. `icmp and dst host 10.1.26.10`.

levels.title: Mission 2 – Filter TCP traffic with BPF
levels.content:
## Objective
Capture a TCP payload and use a BPF filter to separate it from look-alike traffic.

1. Run `lab-trigger m2` while you sniff. Several streams use different ports and protocols.
2. Write a filter that keeps **only TCP packets with destination port 40444**.
3. Read the payload: `FLAG(M2)=<value>`.

**Submit:** the value.
*Report question: why is a BPF filter applied before packets reach your callback?*
levels.solution: `sudo python3 -c "from scapy.all import *; sniff(iface='<iface>', filter='tcp dst port 40444', prn=lambda p: print(p[Raw].load) if p.haslayer(Raw) else None)"` while running `lab-trigger m2`. Submit the value after `FLAG(M2)=`.

hints.title: Which protocol and port?
hints.content: TCP, destination port 40444. UDP traffic to the same port is a decoy.

hints.title: Filter syntax
hints.content: `tcp dst port 40444` (tcpdump / Scapy `filter=`).

hints.title: Seeing the data
hints.content: Packets with payload have the PSH flag. Print `pkt[Raw].load` or follow the TCP stream in Wireshark.

levels.title: Mission 3 – Spoof an ICMP echo request
levels.content:
## Objective
Forge an ICMP echo request with a **source address you do not own** and prove it worked.

1. With Scapy build `IP(src=<forged>, dst='10.1.26.12') / ICMP()`. The forged source must be **outside** 10.1.26.0/24 (for example `203.0.113.50`).
2. Send it (as root) and sniff the lab interface.
3. The server answers a forged request from outside the lab with a reply that carries `FLAG(M3)=<value>`. You can see the reply because the server's traffic is mirrored to your interface.

**Submit:** the value.
levels.solution: Run a sniffer with filter `icmp and src host 10.1.26.12`, then `send(IP(src='203.0.113.50', dst='10.1.26.12')/ICMP()/Raw(b'hello'))`. The mirrored reply carries `FLAG(M3)=<value>`.

hints.title: The source address
hints.content: Use a source outside 10.1.26.0/24, e.g. 203.0.113.50. The server only answers such packets with the flag.

hints.title: Seeing the reply
hints.content: The reply is addressed to the forged address. Sniff `icmp and src host 10.1.26.12` while you send.

hints.title: Scapy skeleton
hints.content: `send(IP(src='203.0.113.50', dst='10.1.26.12')/ICMP())` and `sniff(iface=..., filter='icmp and src host 10.1.26.12')`.

levels.title: Mission 4 – Write a traceroute
levels.content:
## Objective
Write a traceroute with Scapy: send ICMP echo requests with increasing TTL to **172.31.3.2** (a host behind the router) and read the answers.

1. Send one probe per TTL (1, 2, 3, ...) with `sr1(IP(dst='172.31.3.2', ttl=t)/ICMP(), timeout=2)`.
2. Print the address that answers each probe (ICMP *time exceeded* from every router on the way).
3. When the destination itself answers, its reply carries `FLAG(M4)=<value>`.

**Submit:** the value.
*Report question: how many hops are there, and why can you not estimate the distance to the destination from a single reply?*
levels.solution:
```python
for ttl in range(1, 10):
    r = sr1(IP(dst='172.31.3.2', ttl=ttl)/ICMP(), timeout=2, verbose=False)
    ...
```
Hops: 10.1.26.1, 172.31.1.2, 172.31.2.2, then 172.31.3.2 (hop 4) answers with the flag.

hints.title: Which target?
hints.content: 172.31.3.2. It is reached through the router (10.1.26.1) and two more routers.

hints.title: TTL
hints.content: Start at TTL 1 and increase by one until the answer comes from 172.31.3.2 itself.

levels.title: Mission 5 – Sniff and then spoof
levels.content:
## Objective
Write a program that sniffs ICMP echo requests and immediately sends **forged echo replies**, so that hosts that do not exist seem to answer.

1. Start your program (as root) on the attacker.
2. Run `lab-trigger m5`. The client pings three targets: a non-existing Internet host (192.0.2.99), a non-existing LAN host (10.1.26.99) and 8.8.8.8.
3. When your program answers the pings of the Internet hosts, `lab-trigger m5` prints `FLAG(M5)=<value>`. The result is shown in your terminal.

**Submit:** the value.
levels.solution:
```python
def spoof(p):
    if p[IP].src=='10.1.26.11' and p[ICMP].type==8 and p[IP].dst!='10.1.26.12':
        r = IP(src=p[IP].dst, dst=p[IP].src)/ICMP(type=0, id=p[ICMP].id, seq=p[ICMP].seq)
        if p.haslayer(Raw): r = r/p[Raw].load
        send(r)
sniff(iface=IFACE, filter='icmp and icmp[icmptype]==8', prn=spoof)
```
Then `lab-trigger m5` prints the flag.

hints.title: Idea
hints.content: Sniff `icmp[icmptype]==8` requests coming from the client (10.1.26.11) and build the matching reply.

hints.title: The reply
hints.content: Swap source and destination, use type 0 (echo reply) and copy `id`, `seq` and the payload from the request.

hints.title: Scope
hints.content: Answer requests whose source is 10.1.26.11 and whose destination is not the server (10.1.26.12). Run the program before `lab-trigger m5`.

levels.title: Mission 6 – Write a C sniffer with libpcap
levels.content:
## Objective
Write a sniffer in C with libpcap.

1. Open the lab interface with `pcap_open_live()` (promiscuous mode).
2. Compile and set the BPF filter `udp dst port 40445` (`pcap_compile`, `pcap_setfilter`).
3. Capture with `pcap_loop()` and print the source, destination and UDP payload.
4. Compile: `gcc sniffer.c -o sniffer -lpcap`. Run: `sudo ./sniffer`, then `lab-trigger m6`.
5. The payload is `FLAG(M6)=<value>`. Other UDP datagrams are decoys.

**Submit:** the value.
levels.solution: See the reference solution `m6_sniffer.c`: filter `udp dst port 40445`, callback prints `%.*s` of the payload. Submit the value after `FLAG(M6)=`.

hints.title: Libraries
hints.content: `#include <pcap.h>`, link with `-lpcap`.

hints.title: Capture sequence
hints.content: `pcap_open_live` → `pcap_compile` → `pcap_setfilter` → `pcap_loop` with a callback.

hints.title: Parsing
hints.content: The Ethernet header is 14 bytes; the IP header length is `ip_hl*4`; the UDP header is 8 bytes. The payload follows.

levels.title: Mission 7 – Eavesdrop on a Telnet login
levels.content:
## Objective
Show why Telnet is unsafe: recover a password sent in plain text.

1. Capture TCP port 23 (tcpdump, Scapy or Wireshark *Follow TCP stream*).
2. Run `lab-trigger m7`. The client logs in twice to the Telnet service of the attacker with different accounts.
3. Find the password used for the account **labuser**.

**Submit:** the password of `labuser`.
levels.solution: `sudo tcpdump -ni <iface> -A 'tcp dst port 23'` or Wireshark → Follow TCP Stream, while running `lab-trigger m7`. The line after `labuser` is the password.

hints.title: Port
hints.content: Telnet is TCP port 23.

hints.title: Two logins
hints.content: Only one of the two logins uses the account `labuser`; the other password is wrong.

hints.title: Where
hints.content: Keystrokes are sent line by line: the user name first, the password in the next packet.

levels.title: Mission 8 – Build a packet with C raw sockets
levels.content:
## Objective
Build an IPv4 ICMP echo request with a C raw socket (`IP_HDRINCL`), field by field.

The server answers only a **correct** packet:
- source address: your own (10.1.26.10), destination 10.1.26.12
- ICMP type 8 (echo request), code 0
- IP identification field **0x1337**
- payload starting with `NETSEC`
- valid IP header checksum and valid ICMP checksum

Sniff the lab interface: the reply contains `FLAG(M8)=<value>`.

**Submit:** the value.
*Report question: explain byte order (htons) and how the Internet checksum is computed.*
levels.solution: See the reference solution `m8_rawsock.c`. Sniff `icmp and src host 10.1.26.12` while running it as root; the reply carries `FLAG(M8)=<value>`.

hints.title: Raw socket
hints.content: `socket(AF_INET, SOCK_RAW, IPPROTO_RAW)` and `setsockopt(IP_HDRINCL)`. You fill in the IP header yourself.

hints.title: Fields
hints.content: `ip_id = htons(0x1337)`, `ip_p = IPPROTO_ICMP`, `ip_len` = total length, ICMP `type = 8`.

hints.title: Checksums
hints.content: Compute the ICMP checksum over the ICMP header + payload first, then the IP header checksum. Sum 16-bit words, fold the carry, invert.
